name: Consulting-style communication
description: Conclusion-led, evidence-bound communication for executive decisions and structured problem solving.

principles: Organize the deck around the audience's question or decision.
Establish a governing answer or conclusion where the evidence supports one.
Build a coherent argument spine in which each slide advances the reasoning.
A reader should be able to recover the core argument from slide messages alone.
Avoid slides that repeat information without advancing the argument.
diagnostics: Does every section advance a distinct phase of the argument?
Does the message chain recover the governing answer?
Are claims sequenced according to audience decision needs?

principles: Treat each slide as an argument unit instead of a content container.
Give each slide one dominant audience takeaway supported by several concepts and evidence units.
Distinguish claims, evidence, context, qualification, and recommendation.
Make explicit what evidence supports which claim.
Preserve comparison, sequence, contribution, hierarchy, causality, dependency, and parallelism when supported.
Use MECE as a diagnostic when a set is intended as a complete decomposition.
diagnostics: What should the audience believe, understand, or decide after this slide?
Which evidence supports the dominant claim?
Does every element advance or qualify the takeaway?

principles: Let semantic relationships drive visual relationships.
Semantically parallel elements should normally read as visual peers.
Hierarchical or dependent elements should not receive equal visual status.
Emphasis should follow argumentative importance.
Prefer a visual explanation of relationships over disconnected containers.
Use exhibits because they prove or explain something.
Preserve design freedom and avoid prescribing a chart, matrix, column count, or component unless analytically required.
diagnostics: Are claims, evidence, qualifications, and recommendations visually distinguishable?
Are parallel, dependent, and causal relationships visually apparent?
Is anything visually prominent without corresponding argumentative importance?

principles: Prefer conclusion-led and specific slide messages over topic labels where appropriate.
Keep language economical and decision-relevant.
Avoid generic framing, redundant exposition, and unsupported certainty.
Supporting copy should earn its space by advancing or qualifying the message.
writing.title_policy: Use conclusion-led message titles for information-bearing slides when evidence supports a conclusion. Use concise structural labels for covers and section dividers.

questions: Can the audience identify the main takeaway quickly?
Does every major element contribute to that takeaway?
Is the claim supported by the evidence shown?
Are the semantic relationships visually obvious?
Does the slide advance the deck's argument?
Is anything visually prominent without corresponding argumentative importance?
deck_diagnostics: Can the core argument be recovered by reading only slide messages?
Does every slide advance the argument spine?
Are evidence and recommendations linked explicitly?
Are repeated slides or redundant argument moves present?

anti_patterns: content dump without a governing message
several unrelated conclusions on one slide
visual equality for semantically unequal information
arbitrary boxes or cards with no relationship logic
exhibit chosen because it is familiar instead of because it communicates the relationship
repetitive slides that do not advance the storyline
design_freedom: Do not force conventional consulting archetypes when another visual structure communicates the semantic relationships more effectively.
The argument spine controls why each slide exists and does not prescribe its visual archetype.
